first.rationale: Two of the three pressures this quarter are funnel-mechanics problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly moves both. memory_86 and memory_31 point the same direction, which is why I want them verified rather than trusted: both are consolidated summaries whose surviving language is about completion, time-to-value, and first-week activation — all upstream proxies. Neither summary states whether the original experiments tracked downstream qualified revenue, retention, or lead quality, and 'fewer required fields at signup' is exactly the intervention that can lift activation counts while degrading the quality of the accounts being activated. If the archived records show the lift was measured only at the top of the funnel, my confidence in this direction should drop substantially and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44, the one inherited claim explicitly about pipeline quality) becomes more attractive. I am deliberately not choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 reports acquisition and revenue lift but says nothing about the durability of discount-acquired SMB accounts, and matching a price attack is the most likely way to buy unqualified revenue against a long-term-qualified-revenue objective. activation_messaging (memory_91) is a reasonable second choice but treats a symptom downstream of the onboarding drop. Running this as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout because the inherited evidence is 50-64 days old, predates the competitor's move, and the market that produced it may no longer be the market I am operating in; guardrails should include downstream conversion and retention on the affected cohort, not just completion rate, and I should hold the possibility that the observed declines are competitor-driven mix shift rather than funnel degradation, in which case no onboarding change will recover them.

final.rationale: Verification largely supported the direction and, importantly, addressed the specific failure mode I was worried about. exp_86 (shortened onboarding) measured not just completion +13% but time-to-value -2.1 days and 30-day retention +3% — the downstream indicator moved the right way, so this is not a case of a top-of-funnel metric being inflated at the expense of account quality. exp_31 is weaker support than its consolidated summary implied: signup +15% and activation +9% compressed to only +4% qualified revenue with retention -1%, meaning most of the raw signup lift did not survive to value, and the record explicitly notes it did not replicate outside SMB. So I am anchoring this week on the onboarding-flow shortening (exp_86 pattern), not on stripping signup fields (exp_31 pattern); the latter is the discount-like version of this intervention and I am not running it. This also addresses the two mechanically-linked declines at once, since onboarding sits upstream of activation. I continue to decline promotional_pricing: memory_73's acquisition and revenue lift was never verified for durability, and matching a competitor's entry price is the most direct route to buying revenue that does not qualify as sustainable. enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) remains the strongest untested alternative on pipeline quality and is my recommendation for next week's slot regardless of this outcome. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving with this decision: both source experiments predate the competitor launch by roughly a month, and if the quarter's declines are driven by price-sensitive accounts leaving rather than by funnel friction, a cleaner onboarding flow will not recover them. Running at standard scale rather than broad rollout for that reason, with success judged on 30-day retention and qualified revenue in the treated cohort — not on completion or activation rate alone, since exp_31 shows how much of an activation lift can evaporate before it reaches revenue.
